chapters.title: Chapter 5: Where Kelly Breaks Down, and Putting It Together

lessons.title: Kelly's Hidden Assumptions: Fat Tails, Regime Change, and Correlation Breakdown

children.text: Every formula in this course rests on assumptions that were stated once, briefly, and then set aside to get on with the calculation. This lesson names three of the most important ones explicitly and shows, with real numbers, what happens when markets don't cooperate. None of this makes Kelly wrong. It explains exactly why the safety margins from Chapter 3 are standard practice, not optional caution.
Assumption 1: Returns Behave Like a Quadratic (No Fat Tails)

Lesson 2.3's growth formula, g(f) ≈ fμ − f²σ²/2, is a Taylor approximation of the true expression, ln(1+fr). The approximation is excellent for small, everyday moves. It gets worse, in a specific and dangerous direction, as the position size f and the size of a single move r both grow.

body.caption: Exact log-growth vs the quadratic approximation, for one realized return

body.text: The approximation is never optimistic in the other direction. As position size and move size both grow, the exact log loss is always worse than the quadratic formula suggests, because ln(1+fr) genuinely diverges toward negative infinity as fr approaches −1, while the truncated quadratic does not. Real market returns, especially for individual stocks and short-dated options, show far more extreme moves than a normal distribution predicts; this is the well-documented "fat tails" property of financial returns. The formulas in this course are most trustworthy exactly where fractional Kelly already keeps you: modest f, away from extreme single-move risk.

body.title: Compute the exact figure
body.prompt: Using the exact formula ln(1 + fr), what is the log-growth contribution from a single trade with f = 0.5 and r = −0.70? Round to four decimal places.
body.explanation: 1 + fr = 1 + (0.5 × −0.70) = 1 − 0.35 = 0.65. ln(0.65) ≈ −0.4308. The quadratic approximation would give −0.35 − (0.35²)/2 = −0.4113, understating the true loss by roughly 4.5%.

children.text: Assumption 2: p, b, μ, and σ Stay Constant (No Regime Change)

Lesson 3.3's confidence intervals answer one specific question: given that the underlying process is stable, how much does a finite sample leave the estimate uncertain? They say nothing about a different, harder problem: what if the underlying process itself changes? A win rate measured honestly on 250 trades from 2020 to 2023 can still be the wrong number for 2026, if options volumes, participant mix, or volatility regimes have shifted enough in between. Sampling error and regime change are different problems, and only the first one has a clean formula in this course.

body.text: A tight confidence interval is not protection against regime change; it only means the sample was large. A system with 2,000 backtested trades and a razor-thin confidence interval can still be sized on a p that no longer describes the market it's trading in today, if that market has genuinely changed since the data was collected.

children.text: Assumption 3: The Covariance Matrix Is Stable (No Correlation Breakdown)

Lesson 4.3's two-asset example used ρ = 0.6 between Nifty futures and a bank stock, giving f1* = 203.1% and f2* = 78.1%, both comfortably long. Correlations between assets are well known to rise sharply during market crises, often converging toward 1 exactly when a portfolio most needs its diversification to hold. Recompute the same two positions assuming a crisis pushes ρ to 0.9.

body.caption: The same two positions, planned correlation vs crisis correlation

body.text: At ρ = 0.9, the properly recalculated fraction for the bank stock is not just smaller, it flips negative: the formula would now say to short it rather than hold it long, because it has become almost entirely redundant with the Nifty position. A trader who sized for ρ = 0.6 and holds both positions long through a crisis where correlation actually reaches 0.9 is carrying meaningfully more concentrated, single-factor risk than their original sizing accounted for, at precisely the moment that risk is most costly.

body.title: Interpret the correlation breakdown
body.scenario: A trader built a diversified-looking portfolio using Lesson 4.3's method, assuming ρ = 0.6 between their two main positions. During a sharp market selloff, realized correlation between the two jumps to 0.9.
body.prompt: In plain terms, what actually happened to this trader's real diversification during the selloff, and why doesn't their original sizing protect them from it?
body.modelAnswer: Their diversification benefit largely evaporated exactly when the selloff began. The 203.1%/78.1% split was correctly sized for a world where the two positions only partly moved together; during the selloff they moved together far more than that, closer to the ρ = 0.9 scenario, where the second position contributes almost no independent risk reduction and the formula would actually prefer shorting it. The original sizing was correct for the correlation regime it was calculated under; it offers no protection once that regime itself changes, because the covariance matrix used in the calculation is just as much an assumption as p, b, μ, or σ elsewhere in this course.

body.title: Sampling error vs regime change
body.question: A trader has a very tight, reassuring confidence interval around their win rate, based on 2,000 backtested trades. Does this protect them against regime change?
options: Yes, a large enough sample eliminates all sizing risk
No, a tight confidence interval only reflects sample size; it says nothing about whether the underlying process has since changed
Yes, but only if the trades span at least five years
No, confidence intervals are never useful for position sizing
body.explanation: Confidence intervals quantify uncertainty from having a finite sample, under the assumption that the process generating the data is stable. A large sample narrows that specific kind of uncertainty but says nothing about whether the market itself has shifted since the data was collected. Regime change is a separate risk that this lesson's tools do not resolve on their own.

children.text: What Practitioners Actually Do About This

Fractional Kelly from Chapter 3 turns out to be a general-purpose buffer against all three of these assumption failures at once, not just against the estimation error it was originally introduced for. Smaller f keeps the quadratic growth approximation more accurate, leaves more room for a regime shift before the position becomes dangerously oversized, and reduces exposure to any single correlation assumption turning out to be wrong. Beyond simply sizing smaller, many practitioners also explicitly stress-test: recompute f* under a deliberately harsher assumption, such as this lesson's ρ = 0.9 crisis scenario, and size for the worse of the two outcomes rather than only the base case.

points: The quadratic growth approximation understates the true damage from large moves, and does so more severely as position size and move size both grow.
Confidence intervals address sampling error, not regime change; a large sample can produce a tight interval around a win rate that no longer describes the current market.
Correlations between assets tend to rise during market stress, shrinking or reversing the diversification benefit a portfolio was sized around, exactly when that benefit matters most.
None of these three failures make Kelly wrong; they explain why fractional Kelly and periodic re-validation are standard practice rather than excess caution.
Stress-testing, recomputing f* under a deliberately harsher assumption and sizing for that outcome, is a direct, practical response to all three of these assumption failures.
